record.paper_title: Some Open Problems in Quantum Information Theory
record.context_brief: Maximally entangled mixed states at fixed spectrum
record.original_question: Among two-qubit density operators with a fixed spectrum, the same states maximize entanglement of formation, relative entropy of entanglement, and negativity. Is the same maximizing family obtained for every entanglement monotone, and what happens in higher-dimensional systems or under weaker spectral constraints such as fixing only the largest eigenvalue or the entropy?

evidence.quote: Among all density operators of two qubits with the same spectrum one may look for those maximizing some measure of entanglement. It turns out [VAM] that for ‘entanglement of formation’, ‘relative entropy of entanglement’ and ‘negativity’ one gets the same “maximally entangled states”.

Is this true for arbitrary entanglement monotones?
Obvious variants of this problem are for higher dimensional systems and weaker constraints on the spectrum, e. g., largest eigenvalue or entropy.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Let $\mathcal{H}_A \otimes \mathcal{H}_B$ be a finite-dimensional bipartite Hilbert space and let $\mathcal{D}(\mathcal{H}_A \otimes \mathcal{H}_B)$ denote the set of density operators on it. An entanglement monotone is a function $E : \mathcal{D}(\mathcal{H}_A \otimes \mathcal{H}_B) \to [0, \infty)$ that vanishes on separable states and is non-increasing on average under local operations and classical communication (LOCC). Three standard examples are the entanglement of formation $E_F$, the relative entropy of entanglement $E_R$, and the negativity $\mathcal{N}$.

For a density operator $\rho$, let $\mathrm{spec}(\rho)$ denote its spectrum (multiset of eigenvalues). For each spectrum $\sigma$ (a probability vector), define the isospectral set $\mathcal{S}_\sigma = \{\rho : \mathrm{spec}(\rho) = \sigma\}$.

In the two-qubit case (i.e. $\dim \mathcal{H}_A = \dim \mathcal{H}_B = 2$), it is known that for every fixed spectrum $\sigma$ there is a single family of states (unique up to local unitaries) that simultaneously maximizes $E_F$, $E_R$ and $\mathcal{N}$ over $\mathcal{S}_\sigma$.

Questions:
(a) For two qubits and any fixed spectrum $\sigma$, does the same family of states maximize every entanglement monotone $E$ over $\mathcal{S}_\sigma$?
(b) Do analogous statements hold in higher-dimensional bipartite systems?
(c) Do analogous statements hold under weaker spectral constraints, such as fixing only the largest eigenvalue of $\rho$, or fixing only the von Neumann entropy $S(\rho) = -\mathrm{tr}(\rho \log \rho)$?
artifact.status_search_result: J. I. de Vicente (Phys. Rev. Lett. 133, 050202 (2024); arXiv:2402.05673) showed that a universally maximally entangled mixed state at fixed spectrum does not always exist: there are rank-2 spectra for which no isospectral state majorizes all others under LOCC (or non-entangling operations), so the state maximizing entanglement among isospectral states depends on the choice of entanglement monotone. This answers question (a) in the negative and resolves the main question.

status_evidence.title: Maximally entangled mixed states for a fixed spectrum do not always exist
status_evidence.snippet: For particular values of the eigenvalues of rank-2 states, there is no state that can be transformed to all other isospectral states under LOCC or non-entangling operations.
status_evidence.claim: The maximizer over isospectral states depends on the choice of entanglement monotone, resolving the open problem negatively.

status_evidence.title: Open problem in quantum entanglement theory solved after nearly 25 years
status_evidence.snippet: de Vicente showed that so-called maximally entangled mixed states for a fixed spectrum do not always exist.
status_evidence.claim: The longstanding question is reported as solved in 2024.

status_evidence.title: Maximally Entangled Mixed States for a Fixed Spectrum Do Not Always Exist | Phys. Rev. Lett. 133, 050202
status_evidence.snippet: Published in PRL 2024 by J. I. de Vicente.
status_evidence.claim: Peer-reviewed publication establishing the negative resolution.
